sections: Choosing a topic and making it interesting
Before any section is written: what makes a question worth asking, and what makes readers care.
The first two pages decide whether the paper is read. They have to set up a gap, make it matter and promise what the paper delivers.
What counts as theory, what counts as a contribution, and how to build and position the theory section of an empirical paper or a theory paper.
Hypotheses should follow from the argument, be precise, and be stated before the data are seen.
Enough detail to be believed and repeated, and results reported so that they answer the hypotheses rather than decorate them.
The discussion returns to the contribution promised at the start, and says honestly what the study does and does not show.
Qualitative papers have no boilerplate; these pieces are about how to show rigour and tell the story without a template.
Sentence-level craft and the narrative arc of a paper, from people who edit and write for a living.
Reviewing, revising and responding to reviewers
How reviewers read, why papers are rejected, and how to turn a revise-and-resubmit into an acceptance.

items.author: Davis
items.title: That's Interesting! Towards a Phenomenology of Sociology and a Sociology of Phenomenology
items.note: The classic account of why some theories are interesting: they deny something the audience assumes.

items.author: Colquitt
items.title: Publishing in AMJ—Part 1: Topic Choice
items.note: How editors judge whether a topic is novel, relevant and fit for a top journal.

items.author: Bartunek
items.title: What Makes Management Research Interesting, and Why Does It Matter?
items.note: Asks board members what made papers interesting to them: counterintuitive findings, good writing and real problems.

items.author: Alvesson
items.title: Generating Research Questions Through Problematization
items.note: A method for research questions that challenge the assumptions behind existing theory rather than filling gaps in it.

items.author: Ashford
items.title: Having Scholarly Impact: The Art of Hitting Academic Home Runs
items.note: What distinguishes the papers that end up mattering, from someone who has written several.

items.author: Grant
items.title: Publishing in AMJ—Part 3: Setting the Hook
items.note: The best short guide to the opening pages: hooks, gaps and the promise the paper makes.

items.author: Locke
items.title: Constructing Opportunities for Contribution: Structuring Intertextual Coherence and "Problematizing" in Organizational Studies
items.note: Shows, from published papers, the rhetorical moves that turn a literature into a space for a contribution.

items.author: Barney
items.title: Editor's Comments: Positioning a Theory Paper for Publication
items.note: How to position a theory paper so that a reader sees what it adds, with the common ways this goes wrong.

items.author: Lange
items.title: Editors' Comments: Sense and Structure—The Core Building Blocks of an AMR Article
items.note: The anatomy of a theory paper, section by section, from the editors who read them.

items.author: Kilduff
items.title: Editor's Comments: Publishing Theory
items.note: On framing, voice and the courage a theory paper needs, in a few pages.

items.author: Sutton
items.title: What Theory is Not
items.note: References, data, lists of variables, diagrams and hypotheses are not theory; the most assigned paper on the subject.

items.author: Weick
items.title: What Theory is Not, Theorizing Is
items.note: The reply to Sutton and Staw: theorizing is a process, and partial attempts at it have value.

items.author: DiMaggio
items.title: Comments on "What Theory is Not"
items.note: Theory as covering laws, as enlightenment and as narrative; a reminder that there is more than one kind.

items.author: Whetten
items.title: What Constitutes a Theoretical Contribution?
items.note: What, how, why, who, where, when: the checklist most reviewers still carry in their heads.

items.author: Corley
items.title: Building Theory about Theory Building: What Constitutes a Theoretical Contribution?
items.note: Updates Whetten with two dimensions, originality and utility, and argues for prescience.

items.author: Makadok
items.title: A Practical Guide for Making Theory Contributions in Strategic Management
items.note: Eight ways to make a theory contribution, with examples from strategy; useful for finding which one a paper is making.

items.author: Suddaby
items.title: Editor's Comments: Construct Clarity in Theories of Management and Organization
items.note: Definitions, scope conditions, relationships and coherence: how to make a construct clear enough to build on.

items.author: Rindova
items.title: Editor's Comments: Publishing Theory When You are New to the Game
items.note: Practical advice for first theory papers: scope, novelty and the reviewers you will meet.

items.author: Bergh
items.title: From the Editors: Thinking Strategically about Contribution
items.note: Two pages on asking, before writing, what the contribution is and to whom.

items.author: Shepherd
items.title: Theory Building: A Review and Integration
items.note: A review of how management scholars actually build theory, organised into a few recognisable approaches.

items.author: Fisher
items.title: Using Theory Elaboration to Make Theoretical Advancements
items.note: For papers that refine an existing theory rather than test or generate one; names the moves and when to use them.

items.author: Delbridge
items.title: Editors' Comments: Styles of Theorizing and the Social Organization of Knowledge
items.note: There is more than one legitimate style of theorizing; knowing which one you are using helps you write and defend it.

items.author: Hambrick
items.title: The Field of Management's Devotion to Theory: Too Much of a Good Thing?
items.note: The case that the field demands theory even where careful facts would serve better; worth reading before over-theorizing.

items.author: Shaw
items.title: From the Editors: Advantages of Starting with Theory
items.note: Why papers that begin from theory, rather than from a dataset, fare better in review.

items.author: Cornelissen
items.title: What Theory Is and Can Be: Forms of Theorizing in Organizational Scholarship
items.note: A map of the forms theorizing can take, beyond the propositional model most journals assume.

items.author: Sparrowe
items.title: Publishing in AMJ—Part 4: Grounding Hypotheses
items.note: How to build the argument that makes each hypothesis follow, instead of citing a finding and asserting one.

items.author: Edwards
items.title: The Presence of Something or the Absence of Nothing: Increasing Theoretical Precision in Management Research
items.note: Why "X is positively related to Y" is a weak hypothesis, and how to state stronger ones.

items.author: Kerr
items.title: HARKing: Hypothesizing After the Results are Known
items.note: The original statement of the problem of writing hypotheses after seeing the results, and why it damages the literature.

items.author: Hollenbeck
items.title: Harking, Sharking, and Tharking: Making the Case for Post Hoc Analysis of Scientific Data
items.note: Distinguishes the questionable from the legitimate ways of theorizing after the data, and how to report the latter honestly.

items.author: Leavitt
items.title: Theory Pruning: Strategies to Reduce Our Dense Theoretical Landscape
items.note: Designs and hypotheses that test theories against each other, rather than adding one more.

items.author: Bono
items.title: Publishing in AMJ—Part 2: Research Design
items.note: The design problems editors see most often, and what a convincing design needs.

items.author: Zhang
items.title: Publishing in AMJ—Part 5: Crafting the Methods and Results
items.note: What to report, in what order, so that reviewers can follow and trust the analysis.

items.author: Bettis
items.title: Quantitative Empirical Analysis in Strategic Management
items.note: The SMJ editors on endogeneity, significance, effect sizes and robustness: what they expect to see.

items.author: Bettis
items.title: Creating Repeatable Cumulative Knowledge in Strategic Management
items.note: On replication and cumulative evidence; why reporting enough to be repeated is part of the contribution.

items.author: Aguinis
items.title: What You See Is What You Get? Enhancing Methodological Transparency in Management Research
items.note: A checklist of the choices made between data and results that a paper should disclose.

items.author: Geletkanycz
items.title: Publishing in AMJ–Part 6: Discussing the Implications
items.note: How to write a discussion that returns to the contribution and says what the findings mean, without overreach.

items.author: Brutus
items.title: Self-Reported Limitations and Future Directions in Scholarly Reports: Analysis and Recommendations
items.note: What limitations sections actually say, and how to write one that is honest rather than ritual.

items.author: Rynes
items.title: Across the Great Divide: Knowledge Creation and Transfer Between Practitioners and Academics
items.note: Background for the "implications for practice" paragraph: what practitioners actually take from research.

items.author: Bansal
items.title: Publishing in AMJ—Part 7: What's Different about Qualitative Research?
items.note: How qualitative papers are read and judged differently, and what they need to show.

items.author: Pratt
items.title: From the Editors: For the Lack of a Boilerplate: Tips on Writing Up (and Reviewing) Qualitative Research
items.note: The most practical guide to presenting qualitative data: what to show, how much, and how to link it to theory.

items.author: Gioia
items.title: Seeking Qualitative Rigor in Inductive Research: Notes on the Gioia Methodology
items.note: The data structure that has become the common template for inductive papers, by its authors.

items.author: Eisenhardt
items.title: Theory Building from Cases: Opportunities and Challenges
items.note: How to present multiple-case research so that the theory is seen to emerge from the cases.

items.author: Golden-Biddle
items.title: Appealing Work: An Investigation of How Ethnographic Texts Convince
items.note: What makes an ethnographic account persuasive: authenticity, plausibility and criticality.

items.author: Bansal
items.title: From the Editors: New Ways of Seeing through Qualitative Research
items.note: On the range of qualitative approaches beyond the dominant template, and how to write them for a top journal.

items.author: Pratt
items.title: Moving Beyond Templates: A Bricolage Approach to Conducting Trustworthy Qualitative Research
items.note: Why following a template is not the same as being trustworthy, and what to do instead.

items.author: Van Maanen
items.title: Tales of the Field: On Writing Ethnography
items.note: The three voices an ethnography can be written in, and what each conceals.

items.author: Pollock
items.title: Being Scheherazade: The Importance of Storytelling in Academic Writing
items.note: A paper is a story with a beginning, a complication and a resolution; how to find and tell yours.

items.author: Ragins
items.title: Editor's Comments: Reflections on the Craft of Clear Writing
items.note: Short, concrete advice on clear sentences, from an AMR editor who read thousands of unclear ones.

items.author: Barley
items.title: When I Write My Masterpiece: Thoughts on What Makes a Paper Interesting
items.note: An editor on voice, surprise and the difference between competent and memorable papers.

items.author: Bem
items.title: Writing the Empirical Journal Article
items.note: The classic chapter on the shape of an empirical article, down to the hourglass structure of the introduction.
items.venue: In J. M. Darley, M. P. Zanna & H. L. Roediger III (Eds.), The Compleat Academic: A Career Guide (2nd ed., pp. 185-219). American Psychological Association

items.author: Zuckerman
items.title: Tips to Article-Writers
items.note: A sociologist's short list of the mistakes he sees most in drafts; blunt and widely assigned.
items.venue: Unpublished notes, MIT Sloan School of Management

items.author: Huff
items.title: Writing for Scholarly Publication
items.note: Writing as joining a conversation: who you are talking to, and what you are saying that they have not.

items.author: Becker
items.title: Writing for Social Scientists: How to Start and Finish Your Thesis, Book, or Article

items.author: Sword
items.title: Stylish Academic Writing
items.note: Evidence, from a thousand articles, on what readable academic prose does differently.

items.author: Pollock
items.title: How to Use Storytelling in Your Academic Writing: Engaging Readers and Hooking Reviewers
items.note: The Scheherazade argument at book length, with exercises.

items.author: Daft
items.title: Why I Recommended That Your Manuscript Be Rejected and What You Can Do About It
items.note: The reasons papers are rejected, ranked by how often they occur; still accurate.

items.author: Lepak
items.title: Editor's Comments: What Is Good Reviewing?
items.note: What editors want from a review, which is also what authors should expect and prepare for.

items.author: Tsui
items.title: Successful Authors and Effective Reviewers: Balancing Supply and Demand in the Organizational Sciences
items.note: The review process from both sides, with advice on surviving it as an author.

items.author: Ragins
items.title: Editor's Comments: Developing Our Authors
items.note: How developmental reviewing works, and how to read a review for what it is really asking.

items.author: Seibert
items.title: Anatomy of an R&R (or, Reviewers Are an Author's Best Friends…)
items.note: A step-by-step account of turning a revise-and-resubmit into an acceptance, including the response letter.

items.title: Publishing in the Organizational Sciences
